name: GO Classes DA Test Series 2025 | Machine Learning | Principal Component Analysis | Topic Wise Test 6

question.text:
Assume that we have the following covariance matrix $X X^{T}$, please calculate the first principal component.
$$
X X^{T}=\left[\begin{array}{lll}
1 & 0 & 0 \\
0 & 2 & 0 \\
0 & 0 & 3
\end{array}\right]
$$

  1. $[1,0,0]^{T}$
  2. $[0,1,0]^{T}$
  3. $[0,0,1]^{T}$
  4. $[1,2,3]^{T}$

Consider the following data:

Assume every sample data point is marked with "x" and has integer coordinates only. If we project the data onto the first principal component, what will be the reconstruction error?

Consider $n$ feature vectors $\boldsymbol{x} \in \mathbb{R}^{d}$ that need to be projected into a lower-dimensional space $\mathbb{R}^{k}$ using $k$ principal component basis vectors. The projection matrix $\boldsymbol{W}$ of size $d \times k$ consists of these orthonormal principal component vectors.
Which of the following expressions correctly represents the reconstruction error?
  1. $\left\|\boldsymbol{x}-\boldsymbol{W} \boldsymbol{W}^{T} \boldsymbol{x}\right\|_{2}^{2}$
  2. $\left\|\boldsymbol{x}-\boldsymbol{W}^{T} \boldsymbol{x}\right\|_{2}^{2}$
  3. $\left\|\boldsymbol{x}-\boldsymbol{W}^{T} \boldsymbol{W} \boldsymbol{x}\right\|_{2}^{2}$
  4. $\|\boldsymbol{x}-\boldsymbol{W} \boldsymbol{x}\|_{2}^{2}$

Suppose we perform PCA on a dataset in order to reduce the dimensionality to 3 . Let $Z$ be the data represented in the new feature representation, after performing PCA. Suppose the covariance matrix of $Z$ is computed. Which of these could possibly be the covariance matrix? Select all that apply.
  1. $\left(\begin{array}{ccc}6 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{array}\right)$
  2. $\left(\begin{array}{lll}6 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{array}\right)$
  3. $\left(\begin{array}{ccc}6 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{array}\right)$
  4. $\left(\begin{array}{lll}6 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{array}\right)$

Select the true statements about principal components analysis (PCA).
  1. $\mathrm{PCA}$ is a clustering algorithm.
  2. PCA produces features (principal coordinates) that are linear combinations of the input features.
  3. The principal components are chosen to maximize the variance in the projected data.
  4. The principal coordinates are the eigenvalues of the sample covariance matrix.

You performed PCA in $\mathbb{R}^{3}$. The first principal component is $u_{1}=(1 / \sqrt{2}, 1 / \sqrt{2}, 0)$, and the second principal component is $u_{2}=(-1 / \sqrt{2}, 1 / \sqrt{2}, 0)$. One of your original data points was $x=$ $(1,2,3)$.
What will the new representation of $x$ be?
  1. $\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}, \frac{3}{\sqrt{2}}\right)$
  2. $\left(\frac{3}{\sqrt{2}}, \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)$
  3. $\left(\frac{3}{\sqrt{2}},-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)$
  4. $\left(-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}, \frac{3}{\sqrt{2}}\right)$

Which of the following are typical benefits that might motivate you to preprocess data with principal components analysis (PCA) before training a classifier?
  1. PCA tends to reduce the bias of your classification algorithm.
  2. PCA can be used to avoid overfitting.
  3. PCA tends to reduce the variance of your classification algorithm.
  4. PCA can be used to avoid underfitting.

Suppose the first six singular values are 6, 5, 3, 2, 2, 1 .
What fraction of the variance is captured by the first two principal components?
  1. $\frac{6^{2}}{6^{2}+5^{2}+3^{2}+2^{2}+2^{2}+1^{2}}$
  2. $\frac{6^{2}+5^{2}}{6^{2}+5^{2}+3^{2}+2^{2}+2^{2}+1^{2}}$
  3. $\frac{6+5}{6+5+3+2+2+1}$
  4. $\frac{6^{2}+5^{2}+3^{2}}{6^{2}+5^{2}+3^{2}+2^{2}+2^{2}+1^{2}}$

Suppose we are doing ordinary least-squares linear regression with a fictitious dimension. Which of the following changes can never make the cost function's value on the training data smaller?
A. Discard the fictitious dimension (i.e., don't append a 1 to every sample point).
B. Append quadratic features to each sample point.
C. Project the sample points onto a lower-dimensional subspace with PCA (without changing the labels) and perform regression on the projected points.

D: Center the design matrix (so each feature has mean zero).

Which of the following are true about principal components analysis (PCA)? Assume that no two eigenvectors of the sample covariance matrix have the same eigenvalue.
  1. Appending a 1 to the end of every sample point doesn't change the results of performing PCA (except that the useful principal component vectors have an extra 0 at the end, and there's one extra useless component with eigenvalue zero).
  2. If you use PCA to project $d$-dimensional points down to $j$ principal coordinates, and then you run PCA again to project those $j$-dimensional coordinates down to $k$ principal coordinates, with $d>j>k$, you always get the same result as if you had just used PCA to project the $d$-dimensional points directly down to $k$ principle coordinates.
  3.  If you perform an arbitrary rigid rotation of the sample points as a group in feature space before performing PCA, the principal component directions do not change.
  4. If you perform an arbitrary rigid rotation of the sample points as a group in feature space before performing PCA, the largest eigenvalue of the sample covariance matrix does not change.

Given a data point $\boldsymbol{x}$ and a unit vector $\boldsymbol{v}$ along the principal axis of the projection, the projected vector $\boldsymbol{x}_{\|}$is defined as:
$$
\boldsymbol{x}_{\|}=\boldsymbol{v} \boldsymbol{v}^{T} \boldsymbol{x}
$$
The difference vector between the data point and its projection is:
$$
\boldsymbol{x}_{\perp}=\boldsymbol{x}-\boldsymbol{x}_{\|}
$$
Which of the following statements is/are correct?
  1. $\boldsymbol{x}_{\perp}$ and $\boldsymbol{v}$ are orthogonal.
  2. $\boldsymbol{x}_{\perp}$ and $\boldsymbol{v}$ are parallel.
  3. $\boldsymbol{x}$ and $\boldsymbol{x}_{\|}$are orthogonal.
  4. $\boldsymbol{x}$ and $\boldsymbol{x}_{\|}$are parallel.

In each plot below, the data is projected onto two (unit-length) principal component vectors. We say that a plot is "valid" if the $x$-coordinate (written as "PC1") would be the first chosen principal coordinate and the $y$-coordinate (written as "PC2") would be the second chosen principal coordinate. Which plots are valid?

Why is PCA sometimes used as a preprocessing step before regression?
  1. To reduce overfitting by removing poorly predictive dimensions.
  2. To expose information missing from the input data.
  3. To make computation faster by reducing the dimensionality of the data.
  4. For inference and scientific discovery, we prefer features that are not axis-aligned.

Consider the following three points in 2-dimensional space: $(1,1),(2,2),(3,3)$.
Suppose we project the original data points into a 1-dimensional space defined by the first principal component.
The variance of the projected data is:
  1. $2 / 3$
  2. $4 / 3$
  3. $1 / 3$
  4. 1

Suppose you have four observed data vectors, each of which is a multiple of the 6-dimensional vector $\vec{v}$ with $\|\vec{v}\|=10$. You arrange these data vectors as the columns of a matrix $A$ given by:
$$
A=\left[\begin{array}{cccc}
\mid & \mid & \mid & \mid \\
-\vec{v} & -2 \vec{v} & \vec{v} & 2 \vec{v} \\
\mid & \mid & \mid & \mid
\end{array}\right]
$$
Find the singular value that corresponds to the first (and only) principal component.
  1. 10
  2. $10 \sqrt{2}$
  3. $10 \sqrt{5}$
  4. $10 \sqrt{10}$
